newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: ALPINE SKIING-GHEDINA TRIUMPHS AFTER ACCIDENT AND TRAGEDY.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-GHEDINA TRIUMPHS AFTER ACCIDENT AND TRAGEDY.

text.p: Six years ago it would have been difficult envisaging Kristian Ghedina standing on the victory podium.
A car crash had put him a coma for several days and he had also lost part of his left ear.
Now the 27-year-old Italian appears the prototype of a downhill racer.
"I have the same sense of fear as any other normal person," Ghedina said. "But I have never let fear stop me from doing the things I enjoy -- like skiing and motocross."
Ghedina had already had his fill of personal tragedy before the car accident which almost took his life.
In 1985 his mother, a ski instructor and alpine guide, died in a skiing accident on the Cristallo mountain in Cortina.
"When I am racing, I am sure she is looking at me all the time and protecting me," he said.
Ghedina, who considers the downhill the only true form of ski racing, has an insatiable passion for fast cars and motorcycles, and hates sitting still for longer periods of time.
But away from the World Cup circuit, the Italian, whose father owns a restaurant in Cortina, relishes the domestic life.
His favorite hobby is cooking and his speciality is Casiunziei,a ravioli dish from his native Cortina D'Ampezzo, in the northern Italian Dolomite mountains.
"Casiunziei goes best with red wine, but I don't drink alcohol so I just have water with mine," he said. "My grandmother taught me how to cook."
Before Ghedina left for last year's world championships in the Sierra Nevada, his grandmother made 87 pieces of Casiunziei.
"She told me if I ate them all and won a medal then that medal belonged to her because she provided me with so many carbohydrates.
"I did eat them all so I dedicated my (downhill) silver medal to her, but she never got it because I don't know where the medal is," he said.
This year, Ghedina, who also took the combination silver at the 1991 world championhips in Saalbach, Austria, hopes to add a gold medal to his collection.
"It is not often that a skier has the chance to win at world championships in front of a home crowd. It would be nice," he said.
Ghedina's chances of topping the downhill podium at the world championships in Sestriere, which open on Sunday, look better than ever.
He is currently in the form of his life and has won three races this season in Val Gardena, Chamonix and Wengen and finished second twice.

"I have more experience now and am mentally more mature. Now I can joke around until 30 seconds before my start. Then I just tell myself I am better than all the others. That's probably why I am doing so well now."
Together with the Italian downhill team, he trained on the championship slope in Sestriere earlier in the month and feels his chances of victory are good.

"I can do well in Sestriere. It is not an easy slope but it is also not that demanding. It's not so narrow and also not that fast, it could almost be a super-G. There are no real key points, you can win or lose time anywhere.
"But it will be tough. I think (Norway's Atle) Skaardal, (France's Luc) Alphand, and the Austrians (Fritz) Strobl and (Werner) Franz can all do well there.
"The pressure on me to do well in Sestriere will be immense, but I think I have everything under control. I will not start stressing myself by thinking too much about it," he said.
Should Ghedina win in Sestriere, his greatest desire would be to meet twice Formula One world champion Michael Schumacher of Germany.
"The greatest gift anyone could give me if I win is the chance to meet Schumacher. Then I would also like to drive a F1 Ferrari at the Imola race track," he said.
Ghedina has no problems playing second fiddle to his extravagant compatriot Alberto Tomba, a three times Olympic and twice world champion.
"I am completely different to Tomba. I have nothing against him, but quite frankly, I don't really like his image," he said.
When asked about his dreams outside of the ski racing world, the usually loquacious Italian becomes pensive.
"Well, probably to buy a Porsche," he said after a long silence. "No, let's just say it is to stay healthy for the rest of my life."
